chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan and Ahmad ibn Idris from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, all from Safwan from Ibn Mukkan from Abu Basir from one of the Imams (peace be upon them):

Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Permitted to you, on the night of fasting, is to go to your wives' (the verse). He said: 'It was revealed concerning Khawwat ibn Jubayr al-Ansari, who was with the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) in the Trench. He was fasting and remained in that state until evening. Before this verse was revealed, if one of them slept, food became forbidden to him. So Khawwat came to his family when it was evening and said: 'Do you have any food?' They said: 'No. Stay until we prepare food for you.' He leaned back and slept. They said to him: 'You have been negligent.' He said: 'Yes.' So he spent the night in that state and morning came. Then he went to the Trench and began to be overcome with drowsiness/fainting. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by, and when he saw what was happening to him, he informed him of how his situation was. So Allah, Exalted and Mighty, revealed in his case the verse: 'Eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of night]'.
'Permitted to you, on the night of fasting, is to go to your wives'
'Eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of night]'

key_terms.الْخَنْدَقُ: The Trench (Al-Khandaq), a location of battle and residence
key_terms.الْخَيْطُ الْأَبْيَضُ مِنَ الْخَيْطِ الْ: The white thread from the black thread, referring to the distinction of dawn light from night darkness
key_terms.خَوَّاتُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ: Khawwat ibn Jubayr, the companion mentioned in the narrative

ai.seo_question: What is the story behind the revelation of the verse permitting eating and drinking until dawn during Ramadan?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the specific occasion of revelation (shān al-nuzūl) for Surah Al-Baqarah 2:187, detailing how Khawwat ibn Jubayr’s prolonged sleep during the Battle of the Khandak led to a temporary prohibition on eating until he awoke. It highlights the transition from a stricter, ambiguous ruling to the clear delineation of fasting hours at dawn, a key jurisprudential point in Shia fiqh regarding the validity of the fast if one sleeps before Suhoor.
